lines: Many EPSO selection procedures, and the selection of contract staff (CAST), include three reasoning tests taken on a computer: verbal, numerical and abstract reasoning.
They test how you think, not what you know, so there is no syllabus to learn. Method and speed are what improve with practice.
Each test has its own number of questions and its own time limit, and these change from one competition to the next.
The notice of competition for your selection gives the exact figures. Check it, and set up a mock exam that matches.

In the 2026 AD5 graduate competition, preparation sites reported these formats: verbal reasoning, 20 questions in 35 minutes; numerical reasoning, 10 questions in 20 minutes; abstract reasoning, 10 questions in 10 minutes.
EPSO's own pass marks for that competition were:
sections.answer: At least 10 out of 20 in verbal reasoning, and at least 10 out of 20 in numerical and abstract reasoning together.

lines: Time is the hard part. In that format you have about 1 minute 45 seconds per verbal question, 2 minutes per numerical question and 1 minute per abstract question.
Practise untimed first to learn the method, then use mock exams to build speed.
Spending too long on one hard question. Every question is worth the same, so flag it, move on, and come back if there is time.
Judge every statement only against the passage. What you know about the topic from elsewhere does not count, even if it is true.
A statement is correct only if the passage says it or it follows directly from what the passage says.
Small words change the meaning. Watch for all, every, some, most, only, never and always, and check that the passage supports exactly that amount.
"Some cities offer grants" does not support "Every city offers grants".
Passage: "Evaluations so far have focused mainly on air quality; fewer have looked at journeys."
Statement A: "Most evaluations have concentrated on air quality." "Focused mainly" supports "most".
Statement B: "No evaluation has looked at journeys." "Fewer" means some did, so B is wrong.
Read the question first. "Which statement is NOT supported?" asks you to find the one statement the passage does not back, so the other three are all supported.
Choosing a statement because it sounds sensible. If the passage does not say it, it is not supported, however likely it seems.
A summary question asks which option covers the passage as a whole.
The right answer captures the main point. Wrong options are often true but too narrow, too extreme, or add something the passage does not say.
Passage: "Night buses now run in more cities than before. They help shift workers get home and reduce drink-driving, but they cost more per passenger than daytime services."
A: "Night buses are the cheapest form of public transport." The passage says the opposite.
B: "Night buses bring clear benefits but are relatively costly to run." This covers both halves.
C: "Night buses mainly serve tourists." The passage does not say this.
A 'NOT supported' question turns the usual question around: three statements are backed by the passage and one is not.
Find each of the three in the text. The one you cannot find, or that the text contradicts, is the answer.
Mark each statement in your head: S if the passage supports it, X if it contradicts it, ? if it does not say. In a normal question pick the S; in a NOT question pick the X or the ?.
Answering a NOT question as if it were a normal one. Read the question line every time: under time pressure the word NOT is easy to miss.
Percentage change = (new value − old value) ÷ old value × 100.
Always divide by the OLD value, the one you start from.
Visitors rose from 3,020 in 2023 to 3,330 in 2025.
Use a multiplier. New ÷ old gives it in one step: 3,330 ÷ 3,020 = 1.103, so the value grew by 10.3%. A multiplier below 1 is a decrease: 0.94 means a fall of 6%.
To repeat the same change for another year, multiply again by the same multiplier.
Dividing by the new value: 310 ÷ 3,330 = 9.3%. Wrong options are often built from exactly this mistake, so a close-looking number is not proof you are right.
Share of a total = part ÷ total × 100.
Add up the column for the right year first: the total is rarely given in the table.
Four offices received 1,200, 800, 650 and 350 applications.
Share of the first office: 1,200 ÷ 3,000 = 0.4.
sections.answer: The first office received 40% of all applications.

lines: Average per year = the sum of the years ÷ the number of years. Divide by the number of years, not by the number of rows in the table.
Exchange rates: if 1 EUR = 0.85 GBP, multiply euros by 0.85 to get pounds, and divide pounds by 0.85 to get euros.
Check the direction: here a pound is worth more than a euro, so the amount in pounds must come out smaller.
Dividing by the exchange rate when you should multiply. Asking which currency is worth more catches this in a second.
"How many times larger" is a division: the figure asked about ÷ the figure it is compared with.
The answer is above 1 when the first figure is the larger one.
Office A handled 4,200 cases and office B handled 1,500.
A was how many times B? 4,200 ÷ 1,500 = 2.8.
sections.answer: A handled 2.8 times as many cases as B.

lines: Dividing the wrong way round (1,500 ÷ 4,200 = 0.36), or giving the difference instead of the ratio ((4,200 − 1,500) ÷ 1,500 = 1.8). Both appear as wrong options.
For a total over several years, add along the row for that item, one figure per year. Adding down a column gives a total for one year instead.
In many series, one part of the figure moves by the same step every time: one corner, an eighth of a turn, or one place along a row.
Find what moves, in which direction, and how far.
Follow one part at a time. Track the dot through all five figures, then the arrow, then anything else. A series usually has two rules working together.
An arrow points up, then up-right, then right, then down-right, then down.
Each step is an eighth of a turn clockwise.
The next step turns it from down to down-left.
Picture the sixth figure before you look at the answers, then find it. Wrong answers are built to break one rule, so check every rule against your pick.
Clockwise and anticlockwise look alike at a glance. Check the step between two pairs of figures, not just one.
Some rules change a number: a row of small squares gets one longer or one shorter each step.
Count in every figure, not just the first two, to be sure the step stays the same.
Other rules switch something back and forth: a shape is filled, then empty, then filled again.
Some go round three states instead, such as filled, grey and empty, and then start again.
The fills go: filled, grey, empty, filled, grey.
The cycle is three long, so figure 6 repeats figure 3.
For a cycle, find its length first (two or three). The figure you need then matches the figure that many places before it.
Seeing a simple back-and-forth switch when it is really a cycle of three. Compare figures 1 and 4 before deciding.
Some rules change what the shape is: triangle, then square, then circle, then triangle again.
Others change its size: small, medium, large, and round again, or simply small and large in turn.
The shapes go: star, diamond, circle, star, diamond.
The cycle is three long, so figure 6 repeats figure 3.
sections.answer: The sixth shape is a circle.

lines: Name each figure in a word or two ("small star", "large circle") and look at one word at a time. Two rules are easier to see apart than one picture.
Choosing the right shape in the wrong size, or the right size with the wrong shape. Wrong options are built to break exactly one rule, so check both.
